title: Knowledge Check 11: Lessons 81-90
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 81-90 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: A candidate designs four of the seven scored areas in great depth and leaves the other three with no decisions at all. What does a complete solution require?
options: Depth in the strongest areas, because expertise counts more than coverage.
Coverage of every scored area, with the parts consistent with each other.
A polished diagram, because visual quality is what earns marks.
A finished slide deck, because judges score only what they see.
questions.explanation: Complete is a coverage and coherence property: every scored area needs a decision and the parts must not contradict each other. Depth in a few areas does not compensate for an area left empty, because a missing row is noticed faster than an imperfect one.

questions.question: The four allowed design artifacts each own exactly one job. Which pairing is correct?
options: The document is the record of decisions, and the spreadsheet makes numbers defensible.
The document carries the numbers, and the diagram is where the whole narrative is written.
The spreadsheet is the spatial argument, and the deck stores the decision log.
The diagram stores the requirement register, and the deck holds the NFR table.
questions.explanation: The document leads as the record of requirements and decisions, the diagram makes the spatial argument, the sheet quantifies, and the deck persuades. Letting one artifact do another's job costs minutes you do not have.

questions.question: A candidate plans to present three viable architectures and let the judges choose among them. What is wrong with that approach?
options: Nothing, because letting the board choose among options demonstrates openness and collaboration.
Only a problem if the judges specifically ask the candidate for a recommendation.
A clear recommendation is missing, because leading with options reads as unresolved advice.
Nothing, provided each option is described in the same amount of detail by the candidate.
questions.explanation: Providing options without a recommendation reads as sloppy advisory. The presentation should lead with a recommendation and treat the other choices as rejected alternatives with reasons.

questions.question: A design adds a component to prepare for a capability the requirements never mention. Which idea does that choice violate?
options: Least privilege, which limits what each component may do.
The requirement test, which asks which requirement each component serves.
Error budget, which reserves deliberate headroom below a platform commitment.
Source control, which versions metadata beside application code.
questions.explanation: Every component must be able to name the requirement it serves. A component that only prepares for a possible future need is not justified by any current requirement, so it is decoration built at the client's expense.

questions.question: A design states that the solution must be fast and reliable and that every feature needs near-total uptime. What is the core problem with those targets?
options: They are unmeasurable, so they drive no architecture decisions.
They are pitched too low for any customer-facing application to accept.
They should match the platform commitment exactly.
They belong in the deck rather than the spreadsheet.
questions.explanation: A target with no number, no percentile and no stated measurement cannot drive a design choice or be proven before go-live. A uniform maximum also ignores that business criticality differs between revenue operations and internal tools.

questions.question: A late change request arrives during delivery. Which response follows a sound change control rule?
options: Accept it because a written requirement outranks an architectural preference.
Refuse every change once design has started, without exception.
Price the ask, then reject, trade, or accept and move a named constraint.
Add it and raise the effort later in a status report.
questions.explanation: A new ask is first separated from the solution it was dressed as, then priced in requirement, decision and cost terms. It is answered one of three ways: reject it with a reason, trade it for equal cost, or accept it and move a constraint in writing.

questions.question: A five-year cost model lists only licences, implementation, operations, maintenance, integration and change. A reviewer says the case is too optimistic. What is the likely gap?
options: It omits indirect costs such as organizational load and technical debt interest.
It counts maintenance as a direct line, which is really a one-time implementation cost.
It includes change, which does not belong in a cost model at all.
It is complete, because those six lines are the full set of costs.
questions.explanation: Those are the six direct lines, but total cost of ownership also carries indirect costs: organizational load, technical debt interest, governance overhead and unused functionality. For mature solutions the indirect costs often exceed the direct ones.

questions.question: A simple payback of just over two years sits beside a ramp spreadsheet where cumulative cash turns positive only in year four. What does the ramp reveal?
options: The payback figure should be discarded because it ignores the time value of money.
The discount rate should be lowered until both figures agree with each other.
Most value lands late, so moving value earlier is a financial decision.
Steady-state net value is the only number a sponsor needs to see.
questions.explanation: Steady state does not arrive on day one, so most of the value lands in later years and discounting punishes that shape. Sequencing that moves value out of a later year into an earlier one is therefore a financial instrument, and each month of slip carries a cost of delay.

questions.question: A proposed value line has a unit and a rate but no source and no named owner. Why does it fail a sponsor's test?
options: It lacks a source and an owner, so the number cannot be defended later.
It fails only if the rate came from the client's own finance data rather than a vendor.
It fails only because the unit is not stated as a currency figure.
It is acceptable if the owner can be supplied at the next review.
questions.explanation: A value line earns its place with four attributes: a unit, a rate, a source and an owner. A source and a named owner are what let the number be confirmed when someone challenges it in month nine.

questions.question: An integration service account can reach records because it runs inside the corporate network. Which principle settles whether that access is justified?
options: Defense in depth, because layered controls cover any gap.
Least privilege, because permissions start restrictive.
Zero trust, because origin never grants implicit trust.
Observability from version one, because the access is logged.
questions.explanation: Zero trust removes implicit trust based on network location or system origin, so each request is verified on its own merits. In a multitenant platform the network is not a perimeter you can treat as trusted.

questions.question: A requirement needs an answer immediately and holds the caller until the result arrives. Which pattern shape fits?
options: Fire and forget, because it releases the caller at once.
Batch data synchronization, because it moves sets of records.
Data virtualization, because it reads external data without copying.
Request and reply, because the caller waits for the answer.
questions.explanation: Request and reply holds the caller until the answer returns, which matches a requirement for an immediate result. Fire and forget releases the caller immediately and needs a failure path that runs with no user watching.

questions.question: A small company with one administrator is considering governance-optimized release management. What is the concern?
options: It buys approval and audit weight the team cannot staff.
It removes the protected main branch the team relies on.
It blocks promotion through the sandbox tiers they use.
It is the required first rung on a release maturity ladder.
questions.explanation: The three DevOps models are priced trade-offs, not maturity stages: lean buys speed, scale buys gated repeatability, and governance buys provable change at approval and audit cost. A small team buying governance has purchased process it cannot staff.

questions.question: A request path drops the requesting user's identity right after the experience layer. What breaks?
options: Only the trace record, which loses the requesting user's name.
Nothing, because the orchestrator carries the requesting user's context forward.
Retrieval and tool checks, which cannot enforce access without the user.
Only the model gateway, which needs an identity for provider routing.
questions.explanation: Identity carried through from the first hop is what makes retrieval scoping and tool permissions enforceable later. If the request path does not carry the user, the platform cannot enforce anything and becomes a quiet data exposure path.

questions.question: Retrieval for a summarization feature runs under a service account with broad access. What is the failure?
options: The model will summarize records the requesting user cannot open.
Token cost falls because fewer records are retrieved per request.
The trace will record the wrong model version for each call.
Nothing, as long as the model output is masked before it returns.
questions.explanation: Retrieval must run as the requesting user, not as a broadly privileged service account. Otherwise the model surfaces records the user cannot open, which is both a security finding and a fast way to lose a client's confidence.

questions.question: A client asks which single control most limits the damage a successful prompt injection could achieve. Which one?
options: Evaluation sets on every prompt change.
Least privilege for tools, sized to the action.
A documented stop path with a named owner.
Tracing every request and retaining it deliberately.
questions.explanation: A tool runs under a permission set sized to the action, which caps what a successful injection can accomplish. The other controls detect regressions, limit how long an agent runs, or explain what happened, but none of them caps the blast radius directly.

questions.question: A judge asks why a simpler option was not chosen, and the candidate answers by defending the complexity of the choice. Which part of a scoring answer is missing?
options: The decision, stated as a single clear choice.
The reason tied to the requirement the simpler option fails.
The trade-off accepted, named together with its own mitigation plan.
The cost of ownership, priced across a five-year horizon.
questions.explanation: The scoring shape is a decision, a reason tied to a scenario requirement, and an accepted trade-off. When asked why not the simpler option, the answer should name the requirement that option fails rather than defend complexity for its own sake.

questions.question: A design hides margin fields on a partner portal by removing them from page layouts. Why is that the wrong mechanism?
options: Layouts are presentation, so field-level security must protect the field.
Page layouts cannot be assigned to external portal users at all.
Margin fields should instead be hidden from external users by a sharing rule.
External users never see any fields that appear on a page layout.
questions.explanation: Page layouts are presentation, not security: a field hidden on a layout is still readable through other means. Field-level security is the backstop that protects the field even when a sharing rule is too permissive.

questions.question: A scenario gives 40 million records, a ten-year retention rule and a three-second dashboard. What does a strong data answer do?
options: Store everything in a single object and rely on list view filters over it.
Increase the record limit by moving the org to a larger edition.
Answer with the record count alone, since volume is the constraint.
Split by operation, using a summarized layer and an archive at scale.
questions.explanation: Volume questions are really questions about which operations run over the records. A strong answer separates the requirements by operation: a summarized layer for the dashboard, an operational window with indexed filters, and an archive for the retained history.

questions.question: A candidate completes Platform Developer, Platform Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect, Platform Identity and Access Management Architect and Platform Integration Architect. Which credential does that set grant?
options: Application Architect
Technical Architect
Platform Data Architect
System Architect
questions.explanation: System Architect is granted by that set of four exams, which lean toward the systems around one org and the life of the solution after go-live. Application Architect is a different set, and Technical Architect sits above both.

questions.question: A designer is working the record access ladder and must decide where the model begins. Which mechanism comes first?
options: Criteria-based sharing rules for the exceptions.
Organization-wide defaults, set tightest first.
Apex managed sharing for the unusual rules.
Sharing sets for the external audiences.
questions.explanation: Every other mechanism is an exception to the organization-wide default, so the default is set first and tightest first. Role hierarchy, sharing rules, teams, sharing sets and Apex managed sharing are then opened deliberately against documented requirements.

questions.question: An answer reaches for Apex for a sharing rule without saying why the declarative layer cannot express it. Which trap does that hit?
options: No numbers, because no volume figure is given.
Learning the weights while skipping the scenario stems.
An unresolved declarative-versus-programmatic boundary.
Treating licensing as a procurement exercise.
questions.explanation: The guides ask for justification when custom code is chosen over standard functionality. A scoring answer names the declarative mechanism first, then states what that layer cannot express before reaching for Apex.

questions.question: A candidate plans to present every option considered and let the judges pick the one they prefer. What does published guidance to candidates say?
options: Present one recommended solution, with the choice justified.
Present several options whenever more than one design is viable.
Let the judges choose so the panel feels involved in the decision.
Present options only when each one is fully costed for the panel.
questions.explanation: The published guidance is to present recommended solutions and not options, and to justify why the solution should be used. A menu reads as an unresolved design, and the board scores a decision with its trade-off attached.

questions.question: A candidate spends most of the preparation block perfecting the landscape diagram and reaches the end with an empty numbers sheet. Which practice prevents that?
options: Open the diagram tool at the start so the picture is ready early.
Give the diagram a hard stop so the arithmetic gets its block.
Replace the constraint table with the diagram for the presentation.
Present options instead of a recommendation when time runs short.
questions.explanation: The preparation block is budgeted in blocks because the diagram is the artifact that eats time, so it gets a hard stop. The numbers sheet is where the scenario's call limits, volumes and latency targets are checked, and an empty sheet means that arithmetic never happened.

questions.question: A judge asks a short question and the candidate talks for ninety seconds before reaching the decision. What does a scoring answer do instead?
options: Opens with the decision in one sentence, then gives the reason.
Opens with the full history of how the design evolved over time.
Opens with an apology for the parts of the design left incomplete.
Opens with every option that was considered before the final choice.
questions.explanation: A short question answered at length reads as uncertainty. The scoring answer states the decision in one sentence, traces it to a scenario constraint, names the trade-off accepted, and stops.

questions.question: A candidate is laying out a preparation calendar and has not yet taken the advanced instructor-led preparation course. Where does that course have to sit relative to registration?
options: During the two to four week readiness window that opens at registration
At least four months before the planned registration date
After passing the Architect Evaluation and before the Review Board Exam
At any point, because the course is optional with no timing guidance
questions.explanation: The preparation course is treated as a practical prerequisite, so it must sit well before registration. The two to four week window is the readiness requirement attached to registration, not a slot for training.

questions.question: How does the registration rule shape the way a preparation calendar is built?
options: It is the starting point, so study begins only after the date is booked
It is a flexible target that can be moved at will while study continues
It is an informal goal with no fixed relationship to the evaluation date
It is the finish line the plan works backwards from
questions.explanation: Candidates must be ready to appear for the evaluation two to four weeks after registering, so registration is a commitment the calendar counts back from rather than the moment preparation starts.

questions.question: What sets a mock board apart from a plain timed practice run?
options: A practice run is scored against criteria, while a mock board is never scored at all
A mock board is run untimed, while a practice run always enforces the published exam clock
A mock board adds a presentation and a question session from someone who will not help
A mock board is a written exercise, while a practice run is a spoken delivery with no writing
questions.explanation: A mock board is a practice run followed by a presentation and questions from someone who will not help, which is what tests the defensive part of the exam. Scoring alone does not separate it from a practice run.

questions.question: When an enterprise builds its own AI capability, which layer is it typically owning rather than renting?
options: The reasoning model, retrained on the enterprise's own data
The platform around the model, such as retrieval and identity
The provider's model weights and its training pipeline
The physical infrastructure that hosts the inference endpoints
questions.explanation: Most enterprises should not train a model. What they own is the platform around it, such as permission-aware retrieval, the acting identity, the tool surface, the evaluation set and the logs.

questions.question: A design routes the assistant's data calls through one shared integration account with broad access. What is the correct architectural fix?
options: Route each call under the acting identity of the requesting user
Have the model filter results in the prompt before returning them
Log every call and audit the shared account each month
Restrict the shared account to read-only access on all objects
questions.explanation: Permission-aware retrieval comes from the identity a request runs under, so the agent should act as the requesting user. Prompt instructions and after-the-fact auditing cannot enforce record and field access.

questions.question: An enterprise AI build is over its inference budget at steady usage. Which pair of levers reduces the input token cost?
options: Raise the per-user interaction cap and let more people share one account
Move the retrieval index into the source system to shrink the token volume
Cache the stable prompt and cap retrieval to the top few passages
Switch to a smaller model and drop the evaluation set from the release cycle
questions.explanation: Input cost is dominated by instructions and retrieved context, so caching the stable portion of the prompt and limiting retrieval to a few top passages are the two levers that move the number. Caps and model swaps do not address the same term.
